title: Applying a sand-and-cement floor screed
subtitle: Lay a levelling screed over a concrete subfloor to give a flat, smooth base for tiles, vinyl, or engineered timber
excerpt: How to mix, lay, and float a sand-and-cement floor screed on a prepared concrete base. Covers setting out bay guides, mixing the screed, compacting, floating to a flat finish, and curing.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). Reader's Digest Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK trade practice for floor screeding and BS 8204-1 (open access).

glossaryTerms.definition: A section of floor divided by timber or metal screeding rails set to the finished floor height. Screed is poured into each bay and struck off level across the rails before moving to the next bay.

A mortar of sharp sand and Portland cement, typically in a 4:1 or 3:1 ratio by volume. The consistency should be damp enough to bind when compressed in the hand but not wet enough to slump. A wet mix causes shrinkage and cracking on drying.

content.text: A sand-and-cement floor screed is a levelling layer poured over a concrete subfloor to give a flat, smooth surface for tiles, vinyl, or timber. The mix is compacted into bays and floated level by hand. INTERMEDIATE: consistent mixing and timing are essential, and the result is permanent once set.

The concrete base must be clean, sound, and free from oil, loose material, and standing water. Sweep and vacuum thoroughly. Apply a PVA bonding agent diluted 1:1 with water, and allow it to become tacky before laying screed. Grind down any high spots and fill deep hollows with a rapid-setting repair compound, curing fully before the screed goes on.
Establish the finished floor level by measuring down from a doorway threshold or tile-depth marking on the wall. Pin or screed-in timber rails at the correct height across the floor to form
no wider than 1.5 m. Check the rail tops are level with the spirit level in both directions before pouring.

of one part Portland cement to four parts sharp sand, mixed dry before adding water sparingly. The mix is correct when it holds its shape squeezed in the hand without water squeezing out. Tip the mix into the bay and compact it firmly by stamping and tamping before levelling. Compact each batch well before adding the next.

Once the bay is filled just above the rail tops, draw a straight-edged screed board across the rails using a sawing motion to remove the excess. Fill any low spots and repeat until the surface is flush with the rails. Use the plasterers float in circular and then straight sweeping strokes to close the surface. Aim for a rough sand finish rather than a polished surface, as tile adhesives need a key.

Cover the finished screed with polythene sheeting within two hours of laying and keep it covered for three days to prevent rapid drying and shrinkage cracking. Stay off the screed for 24 hours, and avoid full loading for seven days. A screed 50 to 75 mm thick takes four to six weeks to dry sufficiently for moisture-sensitive floor coverings such as engineered timber.

attrs.symptom: Screed surface crumbles or turns dusty when dry
attrs.cause: The mix was too wet, or extra water was added to loosen a stiff batch during laying.
attrs.fix: Remove the crumbling screed back to sound material and relay with a stiffer mix. Never add water to loosen the mix once it has been poured.

attrs.symptom: Cracks run across the bay after drying
attrs.cause: The screed dried too fast from direct sun, draughts, or heating, or was not covered during curing.
attrs.fix: Fill hairline cracks with flexible floor repair compound. For wide cracks, break out the affected section and relay, covering immediately with polythene.

attrs.cause: The bonding agent was not applied, had dried completely before screeding, or the subfloor was dusty.
attrs.fix: Break out the hollow section, clean to sound concrete, re-apply bonding agent, and relay while the agent is tacky but not bone-dry.
